concepts.short_definition: A powerful computational model that captures anything computable by modern computers; used to define decidable languages and prove undecidability results.
The concept of whether a problem can be computed by a well-defined computational model such as a Turing machine or DFA.
The study of efficiency measures for Turing machines and algorithms, including complexity classes such as P and NP and NP-completeness theory.
The class of decision problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time.
The class of decision problems for which a given solution can be verified by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time.
The theory concerning problems in NP that are as hard as any problem in NP, indicating a central open question in complexity theory about their efficient solvability.
A combinatorial optimization problem defined on a weighted graph where the goal is to find the cheapest tour visiting all cities represented by nodes of the graph.
A finite set of symbols from which strings are constructed, e.g. Σ = {0,1}.
A finite ordered sequence of symbols from an alphabet Σ; the set of all strings over Σ is Σ*.
The number of symbols in the string x, denoted |x|.
The string of length zero, containing no symbols.
A language is a subset of all strings over an alphabet Σ, i.e., L ⊆ Σ*.
A DFA accepts an input string x if the last visited state after processing x is an accepting state defined by double circle.
A set of strings over an alphabet representing the inputs for which a computational problem should output true, often used to represent decision problems.

A computational model defined as a 5-tuple (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F), where Q is a finite set of states, Σ is a finite alphabet, q0 is the initial state, F is the set of accepting states, and δ is the transition function from Q × Σ to Q.

The process by which a DFA reads an input string symbol by symbol from the initial state, updating states using the transition function until input is exhausted, and accepts if the final state is accepting.
The set of all strings from the alphabet that the DFA accepts by reaching an accepting state after processing the string.

concepts.canonical_name: Example DFA recognizing strings with first bit 1
concepts.short_definition: A DFA M2 that accepts exactly those strings over {0, 1} whose first symbol is 1.

concepts.canonical_name: Formal proof of DFA language characterization
concepts.short_definition: A precise, formal method to rigorously prove what language a DFA accepts, beyond informal or semi-formal arguments.

concepts.canonical_name: Set of strings reaching a DFA state
concepts.short_definition: For a DFA M with states including q, Lq is the set of strings x such that the DFA reaches state q starting from q0 on input x.

concepts.canonical_name: Construction of DFA for language with specified property
concepts.short_definition: Defining a deterministic finite automaton that accepts exactly the strings in a language L with a given property (e.g., odd number of 1's).

concepts.canonical_name: DFA accepting strings with an odd number of ones
concepts.short_definition: A deterministic finite automaton that accepts strings over {0,1} that contain an odd number of 1's.

concepts.canonical_name: DFA accepting strings containing a specific substring
concepts.short_definition: A deterministic finite automaton that accepts all strings over an alphabet that contain a specific substring (e.g., 'abc').
A language is called regular if there exists a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) that accepts it.

A variant of Turing machines where the head can remain in the same cell (stay) instead of moving left or right during a computation step, with the result that such machines are computationally equivalent to standard Turing machines.

A Turing machine variant with multiple tapes (k tapes) and multiple heads, where the transition function reads and writes on all tapes simultaneously with movements on each tape, having the same computational power as a standard single-tape Turing machine.

concepts.canonical_name: Computational Equivalence of Turing Machine Variants
concepts.short_definition: The principle that different variants of Turing machines, such as ones with the stay option or multiple tapes, compute the same class of languages as the standard Turing machine, preserving halting and language recognition capabilities.

concepts.canonical_name: Simulation of Multi-Tape Turing Machines by Single-Tape Turing Machines
concepts.short_definition: A method to simulate a Turing machine with multiple tapes by a single-tape Turing machine, encoding tape contents and head positions with separators and marked symbols.
The technique of encoding multiple tapes sequentially on a single tape using special separator symbols to mark tape boundaries.

concepts.canonical_name: Encoding Head Position with Marked Symbols
concepts.short_definition: Representing the head position on each tape by marking the corresponding symbol with a dot, e.g. ˙a for symbol a in the tape alphabet.

The procedure by which the single-tape machine simulates one step of the multi-tape machine, including scanning the tape, remembering marked symbols, updating states, and rewriting symbols with head movement.
When the simulated head moves beyond the current segment boundary, the single-tape machine enlarges the segment by shifting content right and adding a blank symbol to extend the segment.

concepts.canonical_name: Equivalence of Languages Recognized by Simulated Machines
concepts.short_definition: The language recognized by the single-tape machine M is equal to the language recognized by the multi-tape machine M′; M halts if and only if M′ halts.

A model of computation characterized by having a small number of registers capable of mathematical operations and a large memory accessible via load/store operations, mimicking low-level programming languages.
A type of Turing machine where the transition function maps a state and tape symbol to a set of possible next configurations, allowing multiple possible computational paths.

concepts.canonical_name: Equivalence of Non-Deterministic and Standard Turing Machines
concepts.short_definition: The theorem that every language accepted by a non-deterministic Turing machine can also be accepted by a standard Turing machine, with halting behavior preserved.

concepts.canonical_name: Emulation of RAM by Turing Machine
concepts.short_definition: The theorem that a Turing machine can simulate each basic operation of a random access machine, thus can emulate any RAM program.

A conceptual tree representing all possible computation paths (branches) of a non-deterministic Turing machine, with nodes corresponding to non-deterministic decisions and paths from root to leaf representing computation runs.
A traversal method for exploring all paths of a computation tree by fully exploring each branch before moving to the next.
A traversal of the computation tree exploring all runs of length 1, then length 2, etc., ensuring progress and avoiding getting stuck on non-halting branches.

concepts.canonical_name: Simulation of nondeterministic TM by deterministic TM via enumeration
concepts.short_definition: A deterministic Turing machine simulates a nondeterministic machine by enumerating all non-deterministic choices encoded on a separate tape and simulating each corresponding run in turn.

concepts.canonical_name: Equality of languages recognized by nondeterministic and simulated deterministic machines
concepts.short_definition: The fact that the deterministic machine constructed by enumerating non-deterministic runs recognizes the same language as the original nondeterministic machine.

concepts.canonical_name: Handling non-halting runs by adding a simulation flag
concepts.short_definition: A method for ensuring the constructed deterministic machine halts on inputs outside the language by tracking if runs at a given depth halt, using a flag mechanism.

An informal assertion stating that anything computable can be computed by a Turing machine, implying that the Turing machine model faithfully captures the notion of what is computable in the world, ignoring efficiency.
The equivalence of various strengthened models of computation to the standard Turing machine model, supporting the correctness of the Turing machine as a model of computation.
A Turing machine with an additional output tape that only prints strings, used to generate all strings in a language.
An enumerator that outputs exactly all strings in a language and nothing else, never halting if the language is infinite.
The class of languages for which there exists a Turing machine that enumerates (or semi-decides) the language.
A language is in RE if and only if it has an enumerator.
Constructing an enumerator for a language given a TM that semi-decides it, using breadth-first search over strings with bounded simulation steps.
The class coRE consists of the complements of all languages in RE, i.e., coRE = {L̄ | L ∈ RE}.
The class R equals the intersection of RE and coRE, formally R = RE ∩ coRE.

concepts.canonical_name: Enumerator-based Proof that RE ∩ coRE is R
concepts.short_definition: Using enumerators for a language L and its complement to construct a Turing Machine that decides L and always halts.

concepts.canonical_name: Turing Machine-based Proof that RE ∩ coRE is R
concepts.short_definition: Simulating Turing Machines for a language L and its complement to build a multi-tape TM that decides L and always halts.

concepts.canonical_name: Encoding Complex Objects for Computational Problems
concepts.short_definition: Representing inputs such as graphs, matrices, polynomials, DFA, CFG, or Turing Machines in computational problems.
Given a graph G and two vertices s and t, determine if there exists a path from s to t in G.
Given a DFA D and a string x, decide whether x is accepted by D, i.e., x ∈ L(D).
Given a CFG G and a string x, decide whether x is generated by G, i.e., x ∈ L(G).
Given a Turing Machine M and a string x, decide whether x is accepted by M, i.e., x ∈ L(M).
A method to convert each component of a Turing Machine into a finite binary string representation.

concepts.canonical_name: Encoding of States in a Turing Machine
concepts.short_definition: The encoding scheme that maps each state in the Turing Machine's set of states Q into a string of zeros separated by ones.

concepts.canonical_name: Encoding of the Tape Alphabet and Input Alphabet
concepts.short_definition: Encoding the input alphabet Σ and tape alphabet Γ as separated binary strings analogous to the encoding of states, with triple '111' separators between components.

concepts.canonical_name: Encoding of Transition Function in Turing Machines
concepts.short_definition: A procedure to encode each transition of a TM's transition function δ as a structured string using zeros and ones separating current state, read symbol, new state, write symbol, and direction.

concepts.canonical_name: Encoding of distinguished states q0, qa, qr in Turing Machines
concepts.short_definition: Encoding the special states (start, accept, reject) of a Turing Machine with separators to mark these distinguished states.

concepts.canonical_name: Encoding of a Turing Machine as a finite binary string
concepts.short_definition: The entire Turing Machine M can be encoded precisely into a finite string of 0's and 1's, denoted ⟨M⟩, by combining the encoding of states, alphabets, transition functions, and distinguished states.
A decider algorithm that, given a string, accepts if and only if the string is a valid encoding of a Turing Machine according to the described scheme.
A Turing Machine that takes as input the encoding of another Turing Machine and an input string, and simulates the computation of that machine on that input.

concepts.canonical_name: Encoding of Turing Machines and Inputs
concepts.short_definition: A method to represent Turing Machines M and their inputs x as strings (⟨M⟩, x), to allow universal simulation and language membership formulation.
The language of tuples (⟨G⟩, s, t) where ⟨G⟩ is an encoding of a graph and there exists a path from node s to node t in graph G.
The language of pairs (⟨D⟩, x) where ⟨D⟩ is an encoding of a deterministic finite automaton and x is accepted by D.
The language of pairs (⟨G⟩, x) where ⟨G⟩ is an encoding of a context-free grammar and x is in the language generated by G.
The language of pairs (⟨M⟩, x) where ⟨M⟩ is an encoding of a Turing Machine and x is accepted by M.

concepts.canonical_name: Membership Decision for DFA Language ADFA
concepts.short_definition: The algorithmic process of checking if a given string x is accepted by a DFA D, running in a TM that always halts, showing ADFA is decidable.

concepts.canonical_name: Membership Decision for Context-Free Grammar Language ACFG
concepts.short_definition: The process to decide if a string x is generated by a CFG G by converting G into Chomsky normal form and running a membership algorithm which always halts, proving ACFG is decidable.

concepts.canonical_name: Halting problem and undecidability of ATM membership
concepts.short_definition: The problem that for ATM, a Turing Machine cannot decide membership by simulating the TM Q on x because Q(x) may never halt, making ATM undecidable.
A Turing machine that can simulate any other Turing machine M on input x, given the encoding ⟨M⟩ and x.
The fact that the language ATM is recursively enumerable; that is, there exists a TM that accepts inputs in ATM and may not halt otherwise.
A Turing machine that halts on all inputs and correctly decides membership in the language.
A proof technique that constructs a Turing machine that leads to a contradiction by considering its own encoding as input.
The language ATM = {(⟨M⟩, x) | M accepts input x}, which is undecidable and in RE but not in R or coRE.
A proof technique that constructs a new object differing from every object in a countable list on at least one input, used here to prove undecidability of ATM.
The fact that Turing machines can be encoded by finite strings and thus there are countably many of them.
A proof technique that assumes the opposite hypothesis, derives a contradiction, and concludes the hypothesis is false.

concepts.canonical_name: Languages not in RE or coRE
concepts.short_definition: Languages that are neither recursively enumerable (RE) nor co-recursively enumerable (coRE).

concepts.canonical_name: Language L = {(⟨M1⟩, x1, ⟨M2⟩, x2) | M1 accepts x1, M2 does not accept x2}
concepts.short_definition: A language neither in RE nor in coRE, defined by pairs of TMs and inputs where the first machine accepts its input but the second does not accept its input.

concepts.canonical_name: The Language L and its Complement L̸
concepts.short_definition: A language L introduced in the argument for undecidability, with notation of its complement L̸, where L̸ \notin RE and L̸ \notin coRE.

concepts.canonical_name: Turing Machine Construction for Language Membership Tests
concepts.short_definition: Constructing new Turing Machines, such as H′, that simulate or decide membership for certain languages based on properties of other Turing Machines.
A property of a language/problem indicating whether there exists a Turing machine that halts and correctly decides membership in the language for any input.
The halting problem HTM is not decidable; no algorithm can determine for every Turing machine and input whether it halts or not.
The problem of deciding whether a Turing machine's language is empty, i.e., L(M) = ∅.
The emptiness problem for Turing Machines is undecidable; no decider can decide whether a TM accepts no strings.

concepts.canonical_name: Construction of new Turing Machine for reduction
concepts.short_definition: A technique to build a Turing machine Mx from M and input x, which ignores input and simulates M on x, used in reduction proofs.
Denotes that ATM is reducible to HTM, meaning a decider for HTM could be used to decide ATM, indicating ATM is not harder than HTM.
The problem of deciding whether the language recognized by a given Turing Machine is regular, denoted REGTM = {⟨M⟩ | L(M) is regular}.
Proof that the language REGTM is undecidable using a reduction from ATM to REGTM.
The language ATM = {⟨M, x⟩ | Turing Machine M accepts input x}, which is undecidable.
If x is in L(M), then L(Mx) is regular (equals Σ*). Otherwise, L(Mx) = {0n1n | n ≥ 0}, which is not regular.

concepts.canonical_name: The Equality Problem for Turing Machines
concepts.short_definition: The problem EQTM of deciding whether two Turing Machines accept the same language: EQTM = {(⟨M1⟩, ⟨M2⟩) | L(M1) = L(M2)}.
Proof that EQTM is undecidable via reduction from EMPTYTM to EQTM.
A reduction that uses a decider for EQTM to decide EMPTYTM by comparing TM M to a TM M' that rejects all inputs.
A function f : Σ* → Σ* is computable if there exists a Turing Machine M that halts on every input w and outputs f(w) on its tape.
A special class of computable function reductions used to prove undecidability by transforming instances of one problem to another.
A function for which no Turing Machine can compute its output for all inputs; such functions are not algorithmically calculable.
The notation A ⩽m B denotes that there exists a mapping reduction from language A to language B.

concepts.canonical_name: Use of Mapping Reductions in Undecidability Proofs
concepts.short_definition: Mapping reductions are commonly used to prove undecidability and related properties, often enabling refined results beyond undecidability such as membership or non-membership in RE.

concepts.canonical_name: Lemma about Mapping Reduction Implications on Language Classes
concepts.short_definition: If there exists a mapping reduction from language A to language B (A ⩽m B), then: (1) If A is not recursively enumerable (RE), then B is not RE; (2) If A is not co-RE, then B is not co-RE; (3) If A is not recursive (R), then B is not R.

concepts.canonical_name: Proof Technique Using Mapping Reduction to Construct a TM
concepts.short_definition: Constructing a Turing Machine for language A using a TM for B and the mapping reduction f : Σ* → Σ* to show language class membership properties.
The problem of deciding whether a given Turing machine halts on a given input.
The set of all strings not in the language.
Languages that are not recursively enumerable (cannot be listed by any Turing machine).
Languages whose complements are not recursively enumerable.
The specific mapping reduction from the acceptance problem to the halting problem used to derive properties about HTM.

concepts.canonical_name: Reduction of Complement of ATM to EMPTYTM
concepts.short_definition: The mapping reduction from the complement of ATM to the empty language problem, showing EMPTYTM not in RE.
The mapping reduction from ATM to EQTM demonstrating EQTM is not in coRE.

concepts.canonical_name: Properties of Reduction Map Regarding Recursively Enumerable and Recursive Languages
concepts.short_definition: If A \leq_m B, then various membership properties of A imply corresponding properties of B, e.g. if A is not in RE then B is not in RE.
The language HALTTM,\varepsilon consisting of encodings of Turing machines that halt on the empty string is undecidable and not in coRE.

concepts.canonical_name: Construction of Reduction Function f for HALTTM,\varepsilon
concepts.short_definition: A function f mapping (\langle M \rangle, x) to \langle M_x \rangle, where M_x runs M on x and accepts if M accepts, else loops infinitely, serving as a reduction from ATM to HALTTM,\varepsilon.

concepts.canonical_name: Undecidability of Language L of Machines Visiting State Twice
concepts.short_definition: The language L = {(\langle M \rangle, x, q) | M(x) visits state q at least twice} is undecidable.

concepts.canonical_name: Reduction from ATM to L using Machine M'
concepts.short_definition: Using a machine M' that runs M(x) and if accepted enters a new state q forever, showing ATM \leq_m L via function f(\langle M \rangle, x) = (\langle M' \rangle, x, q).
A theorem stating that every non-trivial property of the recursively enumerable languages is undecidable.
The decision problem of determining whether a given Turing machine halts on a specific input, known to be undecidable.
A function defined over Turing machines with a bounded number of states describing the maximum number of steps a halting machine can execute, which is not computable.
The theorem stating that the busy beaver function bb is not computable by any Turing machine.

concepts.canonical_name: Halting Problem for Turing Machine on Empty Input
concepts.short_definition: The language HALTTM,ε consisting of encodings of Turing machines that halt on empty input, which is undecidable.
A language over the alphabet {1} that is undecidable, constructed using the busy beaver function values.

concepts.canonical_name: Reduction from Deciding Busy Beaver Function to Halting Problem
concepts.short_definition: A technique using a hypothetical decider for the busy beaver function to decide the halting problem, leading to contradiction.

concepts.canonical_name: Cardinality Argument for Existence of Undecidable Languages
concepts.short_definition: An argument that the cardinality of the set of all languages over a unary alphabet is greater than the number of Turing machines, so some languages are not recognizable by any Turing machine, proving undecidability.

concepts.canonical_name: Tarski's Algorithm for Polynomial Non-negativity over Reals
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that decides if a polynomial f: R^n -> R is non-negative, based on Tarski's work and the sum of squares representation of such polynomials.

concepts.canonical_name: Undecidability of Polynomial Non-negativity over Integers
concepts.short_definition: The problem of deciding whether a polynomial f: Z^n -> Z is non-negative is undecidable.
A Turing Machine (TM) that always halts on every input, defining it as a decider.
The amount of time a Turing Machine takes to run on an input, particularly focusing on asymptotic behavior as a function of input size.
A formalism to describe how functions grow and to compare their growth rates, particularly Big-O notation which bounds a function from above asymptotically.
A mathematical notation f(n) = O(g(n)) means f(n) is upper bounded by g(n) up to a constant factor for sufficiently large n.
The language of strings consisting of k zeros followed by k ones for some k ≥ 0, which is decidable by a Turing Machine.

concepts.canonical_name: Checking Input Format 0a1b by a Turing Machine
concepts.short_definition: A procedure for scanning input left to right to verify that the input string consists of zeros followed by ones with no switching back from ones to zeros.
The measure of the number of computational steps a Turing Machine takes as a function of input size.
Analyzing an algorithm's running time by considering the maximum running time taken over all inputs of a given size.
The class DTIME(t(n)) is the set of languages decidable by a deterministic Turing Machine within time O(t(n)).

concepts.canonical_name: Single-Tape vs Multi-Tape Turing Machines Time Differences
concepts.short_definition: There is a difference in running time between single-tape and multi-tape Turing Machines, affecting their efficiency.

concepts.canonical_name: Turing Machine Time Complexity Notation O(t(n))
concepts.short_definition: Allowing the running time bound to be O(t(n)) instead of exactly t(n) accounts for constants and minor speedups from alphabet size or states.
The language consisting of strings of 0s followed by 1s can be decided by a TM running in O(n²) time.
There exists a Turing Machine that efficiently decides if input is of the form 0^a 1^b and also checks parity conditions and deletes symbols to accept or reject accordingly.
The language consisting of strings of the form 0^a 1^b where acceptance depends on the relationship between a and b as decided by a Turing Machine described.
The time complexity of a Turing Machine with a single tape deciding a language, in this case O(n log n) for language A.
The time complexity of a multi-tape Turing Machine deciding the same language, shown to be O(n) for language A.

concepts.canonical_name: Simulation of multi-tape TM by single-tape TM
concepts.short_definition: Any multi-tape Turing Machine running in time t(n) can be simulated by a single-tape Turing Machine running in O(t(n)^2) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Lower bound on single-tape TM runtime for language A
concepts.short_definition: For any function t(n) with t(n)/(n log n) -> 0 as n->∞, A is not in DTIME(t(n)) on a single-tape TM, establishing a lower bound for single-tape Turing Machines deciding A.

concepts.canonical_name: Simulation Time of Universal Turing Machine
concepts.short_definition: The time complexity of a universal Turing machine simulating another Turing machine M running in time t(n), which can be quadratic in t(n) for single tape and t(n) log t(n) for multi-tape universal TMs.
The hierarchy of deterministic time complexity classes, where if t1(n) ≤ t2(n), then DTIME(t1(n)) ⊆ DTIME(t2(n)), raising the question whether these classes can be equal for different growth rates.
A measure of the computational time required to solve a problem or run an algorithm, typically as a function t(n) of input size n.
A function t: N → N is time-constructible if there exists a deterministic Turing machine that on input n runs O(t(n)) steps and outputs t(n).

The simulation of one Turing machine by a universal Turing machine may introduce a polynomial overhead related to the length of the machine's description, affecting the precise time complexity bounds.

concepts.canonical_name: Invariance of Class P Across Deterministic Models
concepts.short_definition: Membership in the class P is independent of the deterministic Turing machine model used, including single-tape versus multi-tape models and RAM models, due to polynomial simulation overhead.

concepts.canonical_name: Polynomial Time Computation as Feasible Computation
concepts.short_definition: Polynomial time is typically considered a necessary condition for computational feasibility, although large polynomial exponents may still be infeasible in practice.
A decision problem solvable by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time relative to input size.
A formal language L = {(i, j, k) | k = i + j} representing triples of integers where k is the sum of i and j, with integers in binary form.
Representation of integers in binary form where length of number n is O(log n).
The classical addition algorithm with carry runs in polynomial time relative to the length of the input in binary.
Language L = {(A, B, C) | C = A·B} representing triples of matrices with product C=A·B.
Input size for matrix problems like multiplication or determinant computation is O(ℓ² log N) for ℓxℓ matrices with entries in {1,...,N}.
A graph G=(V,E) can be described by adjacency lists specifying for each vertex its neighbors, using O(|V| log |V| + |E| log |V|) bits.
Graph G represented by a |V|×|V| matrix of length O(|V|²), typically more costly than adjacency list representation but conceptually simpler.
Language L1 = {(⟨G⟩, s, t) | there is a path from s to t in graph G} is in P and can be decided by BFS algorithm in O(nm) time.
An algorithm marking vertices reachable from s by repeated iteration over edges, terminating when no new vertices are marked; accepts if t is marked.
BFS runs in O(nm) time on a graph with n vertices and m edges, since each iteration over edges runs in O(m) and marks at least one new vertex, with at most n iterations.
For integers a, b ≥ 0, gcd(a,b) is the largest integer dividing both a and b.
Language RelPrime = {(n, m) | gcd(n, m) = 1} representing pairs of integers that are coprime.
Checking if any integer d ≤ n divides both n and m to reject if such d found; runs in time at least n which is not polynomial in input length (log n).
A recursive procedure to compute gcd(m, n) that uses modulo operations and properties gcd(m,n) = gcd(m-n,n) or gcd(m,n) = gcd(m,n-m) to reduce the problem size.
The runtime of the gcd procedure is O(log n + log m) because in each iteration either n or m is reduced by a factor of 2, modulo computed efficiently by polynomial-time integer division.
The problem of determining if a graph contains a clique (a subset of vertices all mutually adjacent) of size at least k.
The Clique problem has a trivial exponential-time algorithm O(2^n n^2), but no known polynomial-time solutions.
The problem of deciding whether a directed graph has a path that visits each vertex exactly once from vertex s to vertex t.
The Hamiltonian Path problem admits a trivial exponential-time algorithm O(n^{n+1}) but no known polynomial-time solutions.
A Boolean formula expressed as a conjunction of clauses where each clause is a disjunction of exactly three literals (variables or their negations).
A 3CNF formula is satisfiable if there exists an assignment to its variables that makes the formula evaluate to true (1).
The decision problem 3SAT asks whether a given 3CNF formula is satisfiable. It has a trivial O(2^n * n) time algorithm and no known polynomial-time algorithm.

A theoretical framework showing that a polynomial-time algorithm for one NP problem (such as 3SAT) can be transformed into polynomial-time algorithms for other NP problems (such as HamPath and Clique).
A non-deterministic TM N runs in time t(n) if for all inputs of length n, all computational branches of N halt within t(n) steps.

concepts.canonical_name: Acceptance criteria for Non-deterministic Turing Machines
concepts.short_definition: A non-deterministic TM accepts an input if at least one computational branch accepts; otherwise it rejects.
The union over all constants c of NTIME(n^c); that is, decision problems solvable by non-deterministic Turing machines in polynomial time.
Every problem decidable in deterministic polynomial time is also decidable in non-deterministic polynomial time, i.e., P ⊆ NP.
A language is in NP if it has a polynomial-time verifier TM that, given an input and a witness, accepts if the witness certifies that the input is in the language.
A Turing Machine V that given input x and witness w returns 1 if w is a valid proof that x belongs to language L, i.e., L = {x | ∃w such that V(x,w)=1}.
A verifier Turing Machine V that runs in polynomial time with respect to the length of the input x.
A polynomial-time verifier that checks a witness listing vertices forming a clique of size at least k in a graph G, verifying vertex distinctness and that all pairs are connected by edges.

concepts.canonical_name: Polynomial-time Verifier for Hamiltonian Path Problem
concepts.short_definition: A polynomial-time verifier that checks a witness listing a path from vertex s to t visiting all vertices exactly once, with edges between consecutive vertices, in graph G.
A polynomial-time verifier that checks a witness representing a boolean assignment to variables in a 3-CNF formula φ satisfies the formula.

concepts.canonical_name: Equivalence of NP and Polynomial-time Verifiers
concepts.short_definition: The theorem establishing that a language L belongs to NP if and only if L has a polynomial-time verifier.
A Turing machine that can make non-deterministic choices at computation steps.
The set of strings accepted by a non-deterministic Turing machine N, defined as L(N) = {x ∈Σ∗| ∃w V (x, w) = 1}.
A polynomial-time deterministic Turing machine that verifies membership of x in language L by checking existence of a witness w such that V(x,w)=1.
Given a set of integers A and an integer t, determine if there is a subset S ⊆ A whose sum equals t.
The Subset-Sum problem is in NP; there exists a polynomial-time verifier that uses a witness specifying a list of integers summing to t.
Given item weights {a1,...,ak}, utilities {b1,...,bk}, and constraints B and t, determine if there is a subset of items with total weight ≤ B and utility ≥ t.
The Knapsack problem is in NP; a polynomial-time verifier exists that uses a witness specifying items I with sum of weights ≤ B and sum of utilities ≥ t.
Given a graph G = (V,E) and integer k, determine if there exists a vertex cover C⊆V of size ≤ k such that every edge has at least one endpoint in C.
The Vertex Cover problem is in NP; a polynomial-time verifier exists that uses witness specifying up to k vertices covering all edges.
The conjecture that the class of problems solvable in polynomial time (P) is not equal to the class NP.
A function f : Σ∗→Σ∗ computable by a deterministic Turing Machine running in polynomial time.
A polynomial-time computable function f reducing language A to B, preserving membership, such that A ⩽p B if for all x, x∈A iff f(x)∈B.
A language A is NP-hard if every problem L in NP polynomial-time reduces to A (L ⩽p A).
The language ANP = {(⟨M⟩, x, 1^k) | there exists witness w such that Turing machine M accepts input x with w in at most k steps}, shown to be NP-complete.
The class of decision problems for which a given solution can be verified in polynomial time by a nondeterministic Turing machine.
States that the satisfiability problem 3SAT is NP-complete, establishing the first natural NP-complete problem.
If A is NP-hard and A ≤p B, then B is NP-hard as well.
A set of vertices in a graph where no two vertices are adjacent.
A certificate that lists at least k distinct vertices forming an independent set can be verified in polynomial time.
The problem IS is NP-hard and in NP, thereby NP-complete.
The polynomial-time reduction transforming a 3SAT formula into a graph and integer pair for IS problem.
Creating a graph where vertices represent literals in clauses, edges connect literals in same clause or complementary literals.

concepts.canonical_name: Polynomial-Time Reduction from 3SAT to Independent Set
concepts.short_definition: A polynomial-time transformation f that maps an instance of 3SAT to an instance of Independent Set such that the 3SAT formula is satisfiable if and only if the graph has an independent set of size at least k.
A boolean assignment to variables of a 3CNF formula such that every clause has at least one literal evaluating to true.
The property that if the 3SAT formula is satisfiable, then the constructed graph has an independent set of size at least k.
The property that if the graph has an independent set of size at least k, then the 3SAT formula is satisfiable.

concepts.canonical_name: Assigning Boolean Values From Independent Set
concepts.short_definition: Defining a boolean assignment of variables by examining labels of vertices in an independent set to satisfy the original 3SAT formula.

concepts.canonical_name: Assignment Satisfying Clauses in Boolean Formula
concepts.short_definition: An assignment to variables of a Boolean formula that makes each clause evaluate to true.
The design principle to represent assignments of a Boolean formula as independent sets in a graph for computational reduction purposes.
Edges added to a graph such that no independent set can contain two vertices corresponding to the same clause, ensuring at most one vertex per clause in independent sets.
Edges added to a graph corresponding to incompatibilities from assignments to variables, enforcing independent sets correlate with valid assignments.
The result that the Subset Sum Problem is NP-complete, meaning it is both in NP and NP-hard.

concepts.canonical_name: NP-hardness Reduction from 3SAT to Subset Sum
concepts.short_definition: A polynomial-time reduction showing that every instance of 3SAT can be transformed to an instance of SubsetSum, establishing SubsetSum as NP-hard.

concepts.canonical_name: Encoding variables and clauses in Subset Sum reduction
concepts.short_definition: The technique for representing boolean variables and 3CNF clauses as numbers with digit blocks in the reduction from 3SAT to SubsetSum, ensuring the solution's consistency with variable assignments and clause satisfaction.
A classical NP-complete decision problem where, given a set of integers and a target sum, one must determine if any subset sums exactly to the target.

concepts.canonical_name: Polynomial Time Reduction from 3-SAT to Subset Sum
concepts.short_definition: A polynomial-time transformation from a 3-SAT instance φ to an instance (A,t) of Subset Sum, encoding SAT assignments and clause satisfaction via a constructed set and target sum.

concepts.canonical_name: Encoding Boolean Assignment in Subset Sum Construction
concepts.short_definition: Encoding an assignment of boolean variables xi as choosing ai or bi corresponding to xi=1 or xi=0, respectively, in the Subset Sum problem's number set.

concepts.canonical_name: Clause Satisfaction Representation in Subset Sum Encoding
concepts.short_definition: Using digits in the right block of constructed numbers and extra numbers gj, hj to encode the satisfaction state of clauses in 3-SAT within the Subset Sum instance.
If the original formula φ is satisfiable, then there exists a subset S ⊆ A such that the sum exactly equals target t in the constructed Subset Sum instance.
If the constructed Subset Sum instance (A,t) has a solution S summing to t, then the original 3-SAT formula φ is satisfiable corresponding to the assignment implied by S.
A graph coloring problem where vertices of a graph are colored with three colors such that no edge connects two vertices of the same color.
The set of all graphs that are 3-colorable.
The decision problem of determining if a graph is 3-colorable is NP-complete.
Demonstration that 3Coloring is at least as hard as the NP-complete problem 3SAT through polynomial-time reduction.
A polynomial time transformation from a 3CNF formula to a graph such that the formula is satisfiable if and only if the graph is 3-colorable.
A graph gadget consisting of a triangle that represents a variable and its negation in the 3Coloring reduction from 3SAT.

The coloring of variable gadget vertices representing assignment of variables: one assignment corresponds to red and green coloring in one way, the other assignment corresponds to a reversed coloring.
Triangle of three vertices labeled r, g, b that enforces the coloring scheme and forces the top vertex of each variable gadget to be blue.
An assignment of one of three colors to each vertex of a graph such that certain conditions are met, often used to model logic assignments.
The method of checking that a logic formula clause is satisfied by verifying the corresponding coloring constraints in its graph encoding.
A graph coloring gadget where the colors assigned to vertices represent bits, and the gadget enforces the OR operation on those bits.
A graph construction that cannot be 3-colored if the input vertices x1, x2, x3 are all green, but can be 3-colored if at least one of them is red, used to represent clauses in 3-coloring reductions.

concepts.canonical_name: Clause gadget construction in graph G
concepts.short_definition: Adding a copy of the gadget H(xi, xj, xk) to graph G for each clause Cj = (xi ∨ xj ∨ xk) to encode the clause's satisfiability constraints in a 3-coloring problem.
Set-theoretic and string operations on languages including union, intersection, concatenation, complement, and Kleene star.
The operation of union on two languages L1 and L2, defined as L1 ∪ L2 = {x | x ∈ L1 or x ∈ L2 or both}, preserves regularity; the union of two regular languages is regular.
The operation of intersection on two languages L1 and L2, defined as L1 ∩ L2 = {x | x ∈ L1 and x ∈ L2}, preserves regularity; the intersection of two regular languages is regular.
The concatenation operation L1||L2 = {xy | x ∈ L1, y ∈ L2} on languages preserves regularity; the concatenation of two regular languages is regular.
Given a regular language L, its complement ¯L consists of all strings in the alphabet that are not in L; regular languages are closed under complement operation.
The Kleene star of a language L1, denoted L1*, is the set of strings formed by concatenating zero or more strings from L1; regular languages are closed under Kleene star operation.

concepts.canonical_name: DFA Construction for Union of Regular Languages
concepts.short_definition: Given DFAs M1 and M2 for languages L1 and L2, construct a DFA M with state set Q=Q1Q2, initial state (q1,q2), and transitions simulating both M1 and M2 simultaneously. M accepts input if either M1 or M2 accepts.

concepts.canonical_name: Proof Technique for Regular Language Closure Properties
concepts.short_definition: Use construction of new automata (like product or combined state automata) to prove that operations like union and intersection preserve regularity.
If L1 and L2 are regular languages over alphabet Σ, then their intersection L1  L2 is also regular.

concepts.canonical_name: Difficulty in Constructing DFA for Concatenation of Regular Languages
concepts.short_definition: Direct construction of a DFA that switches from simulating M1 to M2 at the right point in the input to accept L1||L2 is challenging because the exact switch point is not known in advance and may be ambiguous.
A finite state machine where each state can have multiple transitions for the same input symbol and can include ε-transitions which consume no input symbol.
A valid sequence of state transitions in an NFA on an input string, possibly multiple due to nondeterminism.
A transition in an NFA that consumes no input symbol and moves from one state to another.
An NFA run that ends in an accepting state after consuming the input string.
An NFA run that does not reach an accepting state or cannot complete input consumption.
The theorem that for any language L accepted by some NFA, there exists a DFA that also accepts L.

concepts.canonical_name: Closure of Regular Languages under Kleene Star
concepts.short_definition: The property that the Kleene star operation on a regular language produces a language that is also regular.

concepts.canonical_name: Nondeterministic Finite Automaton (NFA) Construction from DFA
concepts.short_definition: A method to construct an NFA from a DFA by adding ε-transitions to enable more flexible acceptance of a language.

concepts.canonical_name: ε-Closure of a State or Set of States in NFA
concepts.short_definition: The set of states reachable from a given state or set of states using only ε-transitions in an NFA.

concepts.canonical_name: Subset Construction Method for Converting NFA to DFA
concepts.short_definition: A procedure that constructs a DFA from an NFA by representing states of the DFA as subsets of states of the NFA to simulate all possible computations of the NFA.

concepts.canonical_name: Regular Language Equivalence of DFA and NFA
concepts.short_definition: The theorem stating that for every NFA there is an equivalent DFA recognizing the same language, establishing that NFA and DFA accept exactly the regular languages.

concepts.canonical_name: Transition Function of Subset Construction DFA
concepts.short_definition: The transition function δ of the DFA M defined on subset S and input σ by collecting all states reachable from any state in S by reading σ and then making ε-transitions.
Proof that the subset construction DFA M accepts the same language as the original NFA N by showing δ′(q′0, x) equals the set of states N can reach after reading string x.
A formula on variables using negation, OR, AND operations.
A Boolean formula that is a conjunction of clauses, each clause being a disjunction of literals.
A CNF formula in which each clause contains exactly three literals.
The language consisting of satisfiable Boolean formulas.
The language consisting of satisfiable CNF formulas.
The Boolean satisfiability problem is a member of the complexity class NP since there is a polynomial-time verifier that checks satisfiability of a given assignment.
A polynomial-time reduction from any language in NP to SAT demonstrating that SAT is at least as hard as any problem in NP.

A sequence of configurations of a nondeterministic Turing machine where each configuration leads to the next via a valid transition, starting from the initial configuration and ending in an accepting state if the input is accepted.

concepts.canonical_name: Reduction Encoding via Boolean Formula φN,x
concepts.short_definition: A Boolean formula constructed to encode the existence of a valid configuration path of a nondeterministic Turing machine for an input, such that the formula is satisfiable if and only if the input is accepted.
Boolean variables zi,j,s representing that the cell (i,j) in the configuration table has symbol s from the tape alphabet and states set S.
Clauses in φN,x that ensure each cell has exactly one symbol, correct initial configuration, valid transitions between configurations, and that the final configuration is accepting.
A Boolean formula that checks that each cell (i, j) in a table assignment has exactly one symbol, ensuring syntactic validity of the row configurations.

concepts.canonical_name: Unique Table Assignment Corresponding to φcell
concepts.short_definition: The claim that if an assignment satisfies φcell, then there exists a unique table TA such that each cell (i,j) is assigned a unique symbol s if and only if zi,j,s=1.

A Boolean formula that checks the first row of table TA, verifying it matches the initial configuration of a Turing machine N on input x, ensuring the first symbol is q0 followed by input symbols x1, ..., xn and then blanks.
A Boolean formula that checks that the last row of table TA contains the accept state qa in some cell, indicating acceptance configuration of the Turing machine.

concepts.canonical_name: Unique Table Assignment Corresponding to φcell, φstart and φaccept
concepts.short_definition: The claim that any assignment satisfying φcell, φstart, and φaccept defines a unique table TA whose first row is the initial configuration on x and last row is an accept configuration.

A Boolean formula verifying for each i that the Turing machine N can legally move from the ith row configuration of TA to the (i+1)th row configuration, ensuring the overall transition validity in the computation table.
A function δ that determines the possible transitions between machine states and tape symbols in a Turing machine.

concepts.canonical_name: Valid Table Filling in Turing Machine Configuration Table
concepts.short_definition: A 2×3 block of cells in a configuration table consistent with the transition function δ, representing a valid local state transition in a non-deterministic Turing machine computation.
A logical formula checking that the transition between the ith row and (i+1)th row in the configuration table is consistent with valid 2×3 fillings as per the transition function δ.

concepts.canonical_name: Satisfying Assignment to φcell, φstart, φmove and φaccept
concepts.short_definition: An assignment to variables representing a Turing machine computation table that corresponds to a valid accepting computation from initial to accepting configuration.

concepts.canonical_name: Inductive Proof Method for Valid Configuration Sequence
concepts.short_definition: A method to prove that each row i in the table corresponds to a valid configuration after i−1 steps by induction, using valid transitions between rows.
A computational problem that asks, given an input, whether it belongs to a specified language (yes/no answer).
A computational problem where the goal is to find the optimal solution satisfying some criterion, such as size or value, given an input.
Given a graph G and an integer k, decide whether G has an independent set of size at least k.
Given a graph G, find the size of the largest independent set in G.
An algorithm whose running time is bounded by a polynomial function of the input size.

concepts.canonical_name: Equivalence of Decision and Optimization Problems (in Polynomial Time)
concepts.short_definition: Theorems that establish that having a polynomial-time algorithm for a decision problem implies polynomial-time solvability of its corresponding optimization problem, and vice versa.
The problem of determining if a 3-CNF formula φ is satisfiable and, if so, outputting a satisfying assignment.
The theorem stating that 3SAT has a polynomial time algorithm if and only if Search-3SAT has a polynomial time algorithm.
A polynomial-time algorithm that, given an algorithm for 3SAT, produces a satisfying assignment for a 3SAT formula by iterative variable fixing.
Algorithms that efficiently find approximate solutions to optimization problems that are NP-hard, providing bounds on solution quality.
An algorithm that finds solutions within a factor of the optimal solution size for optimization problems, such as a 10-approximation for Maximum Independent Set (Max-IS).

A theory studying the computational difficulty of finding approximate solutions to optimization problems, analogous to NP-completeness for exact problems, showing some approximation problems are NP-hard.
An algorithm that makes random choices during its execution, such as flipping coins, to influence its behavior or decision process.
An algorithm leveraging quantum mechanical phenomena like superposition and entanglement to perform computation, potentially solving problems more efficiently than classical algorithms.
An algorithm designed to solve problems efficiently in practice without formal correctness or performance guarantees, often effective on typical or structured instances.
The approach of solving problem instances that have specific structures or restrictions (like planar graphs or bounded degree) which may make them easier than the general case.
A symbolic representation over a finite alphabet that describes a regular language using basic expressions and operations such as union, concatenation, and Kleene star.
The operation combining two languages by taking all strings that are in either language.
The operation that forms a new language by concatenating strings from one language with strings from another.
An operation on languages that produces the set of all finite concatenations (including zero) of strings from the original language.
A single-element language over a symbol from the alphabet or the empty string, which is used as a building block for regular languages.
The set of strings described or matched by a given regular expression.
Operations such as union, concatenation, and Kleene star which preserve regularity of languages.

concepts.canonical_name: Inductive Proof for Regular Expressions' Languages Regularity
concepts.short_definition: Proof method to show that languages generated by regular expressions are regular via induction on expression length.
A method to convert an NFA into a regular expression by iteratively removing states and updating transitions with equivalent regular expressions to preserve the language.
An extension of NFA which allows regular expressions on transitions rather than just symbols or epsilon moves, used in state-elimination to convert NFAs to regular expressions.

concepts.canonical_name: Conversion of NFA to Regular Expression via State-Elimination
concepts.short_definition: The theorem stating that every regular language represented by an NFA can be expressed as a regular expression constructed by state-elimination and GNFA.

concepts.canonical_name: Transformation of an NFA to have a unique accepting state
concepts.short_definition: Modifying an NFA by adding a unique new accepting state connected by ε-transitions from all original accepting states, preserving the language.

concepts.canonical_name: Transformation of an NFA to have no incoming transitions to the initial state
concepts.short_definition: Modifying an NFA by adding a new initial state q'0 with an ε-transition to the original initial state, ensuring no transitions enter the initial state.

concepts.canonical_name: Ensuring no transitions outgoing from the unique accepting state in GNFA
concepts.short_definition: In a GNFA, the unique accepting state has no outgoing transitions, typically achieved after adding the unique accepting state with only incoming ε-transitions.

concepts.canonical_name: Adding transitions labeled by ∅ to complete the transition function in GNFA
concepts.short_definition: In a GNFA, for any two states (other than start or accept), if no transition exists, add a transition labeled by the empty set (∅) to represent no strings accepted.

concepts.canonical_name: Inductive construction of regular expressions from GNFAs by state elimination
concepts.short_definition: Proving that for a GNFA with k states, there exists a regular expression describing its language, done by induction on k, eliminating states to reduce size.

concepts.canonical_name: Base case of GNFA to Regular Expression induction (k=2)
concepts.short_definition: When a GNFA has exactly two states, start and accept, the language is described directly by the regular expression on the transition from start to accept.

concepts.canonical_name: Inductive step example for k=3 states in GNFA to regex
concepts.short_definition: Demonstrating the state elimination method for GNFA with three states to understand the inductive step of converting GNFAs to regular expressions.

concepts.canonical_name: Generalized Nondeterministic Finite Automaton (GNFA) State Elimination
concepts.short_definition: A process to construct an equivalent GNFA with fewer states by removing a state and adjusting transitions with union and concatenation operations, preserving the language.

concepts.canonical_name: Equivalence of GNFA Languages After State Elimination
concepts.short_definition: The property that the language recognized by a GNFA remains the same after eliminating a state and updating transitions accordingly.

concepts.canonical_name: Inductive Proof for GNFA State Elimination
concepts.short_definition: An inductive argument proving that any GNFA can be reduced to a GNFA with fewer states preserving language recognition via the state elimination method.
Languages that cannot be recognized by any deterministic finite automaton (DFA) or equivalent regular language models.
A language consisting of strings of 0s followed by an equal number of 1s, where n is a natural number.
A principle stating that if n+1 items are put into n containers, then at least one container must contain more than one item, applied here to state repetition of states in DFAs.
The limit that a DFA with a finite set of states cannot correctly recognize certain languages, especially those requiring memory for counting, like L1.

A lemma stating that for any regular language L, there exists a pumping length p such that any string s in L of length at least p can be decomposed as s=xyz with certain properties, and y can be repeated any number of times and the resulting string remains in L.
A characterization theorem of regular languages that can be used to prove non-regularity and compute the minimal number of states of a DFA recognizing a given language.
A method to prove languages are not regular by assuming regularity and deriving a contradiction from the Pumping Lemma conditions.
The language of strings over {0,1} where the number of zeros equals the number of ones.
The language of strings with i zeros followed by j ones where i is strictly greater than j.
The language of strings over {0,1} whose length is a prime number.
An equivalence relation ∼L defined on strings such that x ∼L x′ iff for all strings z, xz ∈ L if and only if x′z ∈ L.
A binary relation that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive; in this context, it applies to the relation ∼L on strings for a language L.
A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) for language L that has the smallest number of states among all DFAs recognizing L, with number of states equal to the number of equivalence classes of ∼L.

concepts.canonical_name: Construction of DFA from equivalence classes of ∼L
concepts.short_definition: Given the finite equivalence classes C1,...,Cr of ∼L, construct a DFA that has states labeled by these classes, initial state C1 for ε, transitions defined by δ(Ci, σ) = Cj if x(i)σ ∈ Cj, and accepting states those classes containing strings in L.
A formal grammar where each production rule replaces a single variable with a string of variables and terminals, generating context-free languages.
The process of generating words from variables using production rules until only terminal symbols remain.
The set of languages recognized/generated by context free grammars.
The process of applying derivation rules to replace variables and produce strings; notation uAv ⇒ uwv denotes one step of derivation and u *⇒ v denotes a sequence of derivations.
The set of all terminal strings derivable from the start symbol in a grammar, denoted by L(G) = {x in Σ* | S *⇒ x}.
A specific example of a context free language generated by grammar G1, consisting of strings with n zeros, a # symbol, and n ones.
A grammar defined with rules S → aSb, S → SS, and S → ε generating all legal parenthesis patterns using symbols 'a' as '(' and 'b' as ')'.
A grammar with rules S → 1S, S → 1S0, S → ε generating the language L(G3) = {1^n 0^m | n ≥ m}.
A more complex grammar with rules involving S, A, B, generating the language L(G4) = {w ∈ {a, b}* | number of a's in w equals number of b's in w}.

concepts.canonical_name: Derivation Length Induction Claim for Grammar G4
concepts.short_definition: Claim stating that for all derivations from S to a string u of variables and terminals, the count of 'a' plus 'A's in u equals the count of 'b' plus 'B's in u, proven by induction on the derivation length.
The set of strings generated by a context-free grammar G4 is contained in the set of strings over {a,b} where the number of a's equals the number of b's.
Using induction on the length of a string to prove language membership properties of context-free grammars.

concepts.canonical_name: Language Generated by Grammar G4 Contains Strings with Equal Numbers of a and b
concepts.short_definition: The language generated by the grammar G4 contains all strings over {a,b} where the count of a equals the count of b.

concepts.canonical_name: Closure of Context-Free Languages Under Union
concepts.short_definition: The union of two context-free languages is also context-free, and given grammars for each, a grammar for their union can be constructed.
Any regular language can be expressed as a context-free language by constructing a context-free grammar from its DFA representation.

concepts.canonical_name: Construction of Context-Free Grammar from DFA
concepts.short_definition: Given a DFA M, construct a context-free grammar by introducing variables for each state, adding rules for transitions, and ε-productions for accepting states, producing a grammar generating the same language.
A context-free grammar can be constructed for the language consisting of strings with n zeros followed by n ones, for n in natural numbers.
A property of a grammar where a word can have two or more distinct parse trees (derivations) in that grammar.
A grammar in which no word has more than one distinct parse tree (i.e., it is free from ambiguity).
A specific CFG with variables and rules designed to generate algebraic expressions involving operators + and ×, as well as parentheses and variables.
A tree representation of the way a word is derived using the rules of a grammar, showing the hierarchical application of productions.
The implicit ordering of how operators are applied in expressions, enforced by the grammar structure to eliminate ambiguity.
Determining whether a given string belongs to the language generated by a context-free grammar.
A normal form for context-free grammars where each rule is either A → BC or A → σ, with a special allowance for S → ε for the start variable.
A process to transform any context-free grammar into an equivalent grammar in Chomsky normal form without changing the language.

concepts.canonical_name: Parsing Tree Length Bound in CNF
concepts.short_definition: In a grammar G in Chomsky Normal Form, any derivation of a string w of length n has a parsing tree with length at most 2n − 1.
An algorithm to decide membership in a context-free language by trying all derivations up to length 2n, which can be improved using dynamic programming to polynomial time.

concepts.canonical_name: Pumping Lemma for Context Free Languages
concepts.short_definition: A lemma stating that for any sufficiently long word in a context free language, the word can be decomposed as uvxyz with specific properties allowing pumping while remaining in the language.
Parsing trees derived from a context-free grammar representing derivations of strings in the language, where non-terminals label internal nodes and terminals label leaves.

concepts.canonical_name: Length Bound in Pumping Lemma for CFL
concepts.short_definition: The minimum length l is chosen as b times the number of variables |V| plus 2, where b is the maximum number of symbols on the right hand side of any rule, ensuring a sufficiently long string to apply the pumping lemma.

concepts.canonical_name: Structure of Pumped Decomposition uvxyz in CFL Pumping Lemma
concepts.short_definition: In the decomposition w=uvxyz, the substring vxy has length bounded by l, v and y are the substrings to be pumped, and |vy| > 0 to ensure non-trivial pumping.

concepts.canonical_name: Non-Context-Free Languages Demonstrated by Pumping Lemma
concepts.short_definition: Methodology to use the pumping lemma to prove certain languages are not context-free by deriving contradictions when pumped substrings violate language conditions.

concepts.canonical_name: String Construction for Pumping Lemma Contradiction
concepts.short_definition: Choosing the string w = 0^ℓ 1^ℓ 0^ℓ 1^ℓ in language L2 to invoke pumping lemma for contradiction of context-freeness.
A language generated by a context-free grammar; recognized by a pushdown automaton.

concepts.canonical_name: Language L3 = {a^i b^j c^k | 0 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ k}
concepts.short_definition: A formal language where the number of a's is at most the number of b's, which is at most the number of c's; shown not context-free with pumping lemma.
Languages that cannot be generated by any context-free grammar; some require stronger tools than the pumping lemma to prove.

concepts.canonical_name: Limitations of Pumping Lemma for CFLs
concepts.short_definition: The pumping lemma for context-free languages does not detect non-context-freeness in all languages; some require other tools for proof.
More powerful methods than the pumping lemma used to prove some languages are not context-free.
A computational model with finite control and a stack memory, equivalent to context free languages, typically nondeterministic.
A memory structure in a pushdown automaton that allows push and pop operations from the top to keep track of information.
A transition of a PDA depends on the current state, the input symbol read (or epsilon), and the top stack symbol, causing a new state and stack operation.

concepts.canonical_name: Language L1 = {0^m1^n | m ≥ n > 0} accepted by PDA
concepts.short_definition: A language consisting of strings with m zeros followed by n ones where m is at least n and both are greater than zero, accepted by an example PDA.

concepts.canonical_name: Language L2 = {a^i b^j c^k | i = j or i = k} accepted by PDA
concepts.short_definition: A language consisting of strings with i a's followed by j b's and k c's where i equals j or i equals k, accepted by an example PDA.
The precise mathematical specification of pushdown automata including states, stack alphabet, transition functions, and acceptance conditions.
A function δ: Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) × (Γ ∪ {ε}) → P(Q × (Γ ∪ {ε})) describing how the PDA moves from one state to another, reading input symbols or ε, popping from stack, and pushing symbols on stack.

A sequence of states, stack strings, and input positions describing a valid run of the PDA on an input, following specified rules including stack operations and input consumption, accepting if it ends in an accepting state after reading all input.
The set of input strings that a PDA accepts, i.e., those for which the PDA has at least one accepting computation path, defining the language recognized by the PDA.
A feature to determine if the stack of a PDA is empty, not included in the formal PDA definition, but often used in constructions.

concepts.canonical_name: PDA Construction Fix for Stack Emptiness
concepts.short_definition: A technique to fix PDAs that use stack emptiness checks by adding a new initial state pushing a special symbol to the stack and popping it to simulate emptiness check.

concepts.canonical_name: Equivalence of PDAs and Context-Free Languages
concepts.short_definition: The theorem stating that a language is context-free if and only if there exists a PDA recognizing it.

concepts.canonical_name: Closure Properties of Context Free Languages
concepts.short_definition: Operations under which context free languages are closed, such as union and intersection with regular languages.

concepts.canonical_name: Intersection of a Context Free Language and a Regular Language
concepts.short_definition: The operation of intersecting a context free language with a regular language results in a context free language.

concepts.canonical_name: Parallel Simulation of PDA and DFA
concepts.short_definition: A technique to construct a PDA that simulates simultaneously a PDA and a DFA for intersection purposes.

concepts.canonical_name: Non-Closure of Context Free Languages under Intersection
concepts.short_definition: The fact that the intersection of two context free languages need not be context free.

concepts.canonical_name: Counterexample Showing Non-Closure of CFLs under Intersection
concepts.short_definition: Languages L1 = {a^i b^j c^k | i = j} and L2 = {a^i b^j c^k | j = k} are context free but their intersection is not context free.
The language {a^i b^j c^k | i = j = k} is not context free.

concepts.canonical_name: Context Free Language Non-Closure under Complement
concepts.short_definition: There exist context free languages whose complement is not context free (implied by Lemma 1.4 and its corollary).
The method to construct a PDA that simulates derivation of strings in a given CFG to recognize the same context free language.
The acceptance conditions for a PDA can include accepting by empty stack or by reaching an accepting state, and transitions can be added accordingly to model acceptance.

concepts.canonical_name: Transformation of PDA to have Single Accepting State and Empty Stack Acceptance
concepts.short_definition: A PDA can be transformed to have a single accepting state and to accept by empty stack by adding new states and ε-transitions that pop the stack before acceptance.

concepts.canonical_name: Conversion of PDA Transitions to Push or Pop Only
concepts.short_definition: Transitions in a PDA that do not push or pop the stack can be replaced by sequences of transitions that push and pop a new stack symbol, ensuring every transition pushes or pops.

concepts.canonical_name: Construction of Context-Free Grammar from a PDA
concepts.short_definition: A context-free grammar can be constructed from a PDA by defining variables Aq,q′ to represent the set of words that take the PDA from state q with empty stack to state q′ with empty stack and adding rules to implement this logic.

concepts.canonical_name: CFG Productions for PDA State Pairs
concepts.short_definition: The CFG has productions: Ap,q → Ap,r Ar,q for any states p,r,q; Aq,q → ε for any state q; and productions corresponding to PDA transitions involving pushes and pops of stack symbols.
The mechanism where the left transition pushes a symbol onto the stack and the right transition pops it from the stack, illustrating how the stack is manipulated during state transitions in a PDA.

A nonterminal symbol Ap,q in the constructed context-free grammar that represents the set of strings taking a PDA from state p with an empty stack to state q with an empty stack, without changing the stack.

A production rule in the context-free grammar that reflects PDA transitions: the derivation aAr,sb represents strings leading from state p to q by pushing and popping stack symbols with an intermediate transition from r to s that leaves the stack unchanged.

concepts.canonical_name: Language Equivalence of CFG and PDA (L(G) = L)
concepts.short_definition: The claim and proof that the language generated by the constructed grammar G is exactly the language accepted by the PDA P, showing the equivalence of the grammar and the automaton.

concepts.canonical_name: Inductive Proof Method for Language Inclusion
concepts.short_definition: The use of induction on the derivation or computation steps to prove inclusion relationships between languages of grammar and PDA.
A step in mathematical induction where one assumes a statement true for k and proves it for k+1.

concepts.canonical_name: Computation Path of a Pushdown Automaton
concepts.short_definition: The sequence of states and stack operations a pushdown automaton (PDA) goes through for an input string.

concepts.canonical_name: Empty Stack Configuration in PDA Computation
concepts.short_definition: A configuration in a pushdown automaton's computation where the stack is empty.

concepts.canonical_name: Decomposition of String by PDA Stack Emptiness
concepts.short_definition: Breaking a string into parts based on when the stack of a pushdown automaton is empty during computation.

concepts.canonical_name: Transition Form in Pushdown Automata with Empty Stack
concepts.short_definition: The form of transitions in a PDA where the stack operations involve pushing at the start and popping at the end with empty stack in between.

concepts.canonical_name: Rule Derivation for Pushdown Automata Computation
concepts.short_definition: Deriving grammar rules Ap,q 26; Ap,rAr,q corresponding to PDA computations from state p to q.
An infinite sequence of cells initially containing the input and filled later with a special blank symbol ⊥.
A pointer positioned on the tape that reads the symbol under it, writes to the cell, and moves left or right according to the machine's instructions.
Finite set of states including special states qaccept and qreject that guide the computation process of the machine.
The rules that define, for each state and tape symbol, the next state, the symbol to write on the tape, and the direction to move the head.
The process of designing a Turing machine that accepts strings over {0,1} that are equal to their reverse (palindromes).

concepts.canonical_name: String Equality Checking by Turing Machine
concepts.short_definition: The method of designing a Turing machine to decide whether an input string is of the form x#y where x,y ∈ {0,1}* and x = y, by comparing corresponding symbols one-by-one using finite states and tape manipulations.
The process M(x) where a TM M computes on input string x ∈ Σ*, starting from initial configuration and following transitions until halting states.
A compact notation representing the state, tape content, and head position of a Turing machine at a certain instant during its computation.
A relation describing how one TM configuration produces the next configuration according to the transition function during computation.

concepts.canonical_name: Language Recognized by a Turing Machine
concepts.short_definition: The set L(M) consisting of all strings x ∈ Σ* such that the Turing machine M accepts x.
The set of all decidable languages is denoted by R.

concepts.canonical_name: Turing Machine Design To Decide {0^{2n} | n >= 0}
concepts.short_definition: A method to design a Turing machine that decides the language consisting of strings of zeros whose length is a power of two (0^{2n}).
An algorithm for a Turing machine to recognize the language of strings of the form a^i b^j c^k where i,j,k≥1 and k equals i times j.

concepts.canonical_name: Language a^i b^j c^k with k = i × j
concepts.short_definition: The formal language consisting of strings of symbols a, b, and c in the order a^i b^j c^k where k equals i times j, and i,j,k ≥ 1.

concepts.canonical_name: Language L1: Strings not containing substring '1001'
concepts.short_definition: The set of all strings over alphabet {0,1} that do not contain the substring '1001'.

concepts.canonical_name: Language L2: Strings beginning with 0 and ending with 1
concepts.short_definition: The set of all strings over alphabet {0,1} that start with symbol '0' and end with symbol '1'.

concepts.canonical_name: Language L3: Strings where every odd position is 1
concepts.short_definition: The set of all strings over alphabet {0,1} where each character in an odd index (1-based) is the symbol '1'.

concepts.canonical_name: Language L4: Strings representing binary numbers divisible by 8
concepts.short_definition: The set of all strings over alphabet {0,1} which, interpreted as binary numbers, are congruent to 0 modulo 8.

concepts.canonical_name: Language L5: Strings representing binary numbers divisible by 3
concepts.short_definition: The set of all strings over alphabet {0,1} which, interpreted as binary numbers, are congruent to 0 modulo 3.

concepts.canonical_name: Language Ending with a Specific String
concepts.short_definition: A language consisting of all strings over a given alphabet that end with a specified substring.

concepts.canonical_name: Language with String Length Congruence Modulo n
concepts.short_definition: A language consisting of all strings whose length is congruent to a specific value modulo n.
A language of all strings having length bounded by a certain threshold.

concepts.canonical_name: Language Defined by Starting Symbol and Length Parity
concepts.short_definition: A language where strings start with a given symbol and have lengths with specific parity conditions.
An NFA that has exactly one accepting state.
A DFA that has exactly one accepting state.

concepts.canonical_name: Existence of Decisive NFA for Regular Languages
concepts.short_definition: For every regular language L, there exists a decisive NFA that accepts L.

concepts.canonical_name: Existence of Decisive DFA for Regular Languages
concepts.short_definition: Whether every regular language has a decisive DFA accepting it.

concepts.canonical_name: Language L defined by balancing substrings 01 and 10
concepts.short_definition: The language L = {w ∈{0, 1}* | the number of substrings '01' in w equals the number of substrings '10' in w}.
A binary string that reads the same forwards and backwards.
A language containing a finite number of strings.
A language containing infinitely many strings.

concepts.canonical_name: Language Regularity Closure Under Insertion at Positions
concepts.short_definition: The property that inserting symbols at each position in strings from a regular language results in another regular language.
The language consisting of strings of the form w0 where w is any string over {0,1}*.
The language consisting of all strings over {0,1}* of length exactly r.
The concatenation L′ = Lr || Sr is the language consisting of all strings that can be formed by concatenating a string from Lr with a string from Sr.
The number of states in a Non-deterministic Finite Automaton recognizing a language.
The number of states in a Deterministic Finite Automaton recognizing a language.
